When the Lab Remembers — complete executed research notebook¶

This notebook actually reruns every v1 experiment, every v2 main experiment and every predeclared v2 sensitivity. It also regenerates the measured OPV data analysis, repeats the locked emulator fitting and held-out evaluation, runs the scientific checks, recreates figures and compares the fresh results with the frozen study files. It does not substitute cached CSVs for execution.

The evidence has three distinct levels: measured OPV replicate responses; mathematical emulators informed by measured formulation data; and synthetic carryover experiments. A confidence guarantee for an emulator under declared apparatus/noise bounds does not certify a real material or establish that carryover caused a measured replicate disagreement.

Run this notebook yourself¶

Keep the complete project folder structure. Install the versions in requirements_notebook.txt, select that Python environment, and Run All. The first cell finds the project root automatically; set the LAB_REMEMBERS_ROOT environment variable or edit PROJECT_ROOT if necessary. The full execution takes several minutes and writes a new isolated rerun directory. Frozen original study files are never overwritten.

The executable source is bundled at v1 simulator, v1 runner, v2 policies, v2 planner, cubic emulator, and v2 runner. Configuration and assumptions are in v1 protocol, v2 protocol, and theory note.

from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import os, sys, json, hashlib, shutil, subprocess, time, platform, importlib.metadata
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display, Markdown, Image, Code

def find_project_root():
    if os.environ.get('LAB_REMEMBERS_ROOT'):
        return Path(os.environ['LAB_REMEMBERS_ROOT']).expanduser().resolve()
    for candidate in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents]:
        if (candidate/'research/lab_memory.py').exists() and (candidate/'application').exists():
            return candidate.resolve()
    raise FileNotFoundError('Set LAB_REMEMBERS_ROOT to the unzipped lab_remembers project.')

Isolated source and data snapshot¶

Only source code, protocols and input data are copied into this new directory. The evaluation outputs will be created by the actual runs below. The manifest records the exact files used, including the original workbook, grouped data, source code, protocols and locked emulator coefficients.

In [2]:
def sha256(path):
    return hashlib.sha256(Path(path).read_bytes()).hexdigest()

inputs = []
for relative in ['research','research/v2']:
    source_dir=PROJECT_ROOT/relative
    destination=RUN_ROOT/relative
    destination.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
    allowed_json={'protocol.json','protocol_draft.json','emulator_models.json','emulator_validation.json'}
    for path in source_dir.iterdir():
        if not path.is_file():
            continue
        if path.suffix=='.py' or path.name in allowed_json or path.name in {'requirements.txt','theory_note.md'}:
            shutil.copy2(path,destination/path.name)
            inputs.append(path.relative_to(PROJECT_ROOT))

for path in (PROJECT_ROOT/'application').rglob('*'):
    if path.is_file() and path.suffix in {'.py','.json','.csv','.xlsx','.txt','.md','.npz'} and '__pycache__' not in path.parts:
        relative=path.relative_to(PROJECT_ROOT)
        destination=RUN_ROOT/relative
        destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
        shutil.copy2(path,destination)
        inputs.append(relative)

input_manifest={str(p):sha256(PROJECT_ROOT/p) for p in sorted(set(inputs))}

run_logs=[]
def run_python(relative, *arguments):
    script=RUN_ROOT/relative
    command=[sys.executable,str(script),*map(str,arguments)]
    log_name=relative.replace('/','__').replace('.py','')+'.log'
    log_path=LOG_ROOT/log_name
    started=time.perf_counter()
    with log_path.open('w') as log:
        process=subprocess.Popen(command,cwd=script.parent,stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
                                 stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,text=True,bufsize=1)
        for line in process.stdout:
            log.write(line);log.flush()
            print(f'[{script.name}] {line}',end='')
        return_code=process.wait()
    record={'script':relative,'command':command,'return_code':return_code,
            'elapsed_seconds':time.perf_counter()-started,'log':str(log_path),
            'log_sha256':sha256(log_path)}
    run_logs.append(record)
    if return_code!=0:
        raise RuntimeError(f'{relative} failed with exit code {return_code}; see {log_path}')
    return record

run_python('research/test_lab_memory.py')
run_python('research/v2/test_v2.py')

Measured OPV evidence, regenerated from the original workbook¶

The authors' data are from Langner et al., Beyond Ternary OPV: High-Throughput Experimentation and Self-Driving Laboratories Optimize Multicomponent Systems, DOI 10.1002/adma.201907801. Duplicate compositions and both SDA replicate readings are preserved. Negative degradation readings are retained. The two systems share some constituent measurements, so they are not fully independent material replications.

The declared threshold is degradation at most 0.10. Replicate threshold disagreement is descriptive evidence of measurement/reconfirmation difficulty. Neither reading is assumed to be ground truth, and these data do not identify carryover causally.

Published resource and carryover context¶

These primary-source tables are contextual evidence, not a transfer calibration. The OPV publication reports batch preparation and processing durations; overlapping batch processes cannot be summed to infer a marginal fresh/routine assay-cost ratio. The separate AutoFSP measurements use a different apparatus and a different carryover definition, so they are not a calibration of the OPV retained-mass fraction. All simulated cost ratios and apparatus bounds remain declared assumptions.

Response emulator: grouped development selection and untouched held-out fidelity¶

The primary family is a prespecified cubic Bernstein polynomial. Ridge strength is selected using validation composition groups only; the family is not changed after seeing held-out accuracy. The final train+validation fit is locked before its test error is computed. A separate, predeclared piecewise-affine interpolator supplies an emulator-sensitivity case.

For degree (p), the emulator's full-simplex L1 certificate is

[ L=\frac p2\max_{|\gamma|=p-1,i,j}|\beta_{\gamma+e_i}-\beta_{\gamma+e_j}|. ]

This follows from the range of the directional derivative on the simplex tangent space. It certifies this mathematical emulator only. Empirical pairwise slopes do not provide a valid upper bound for an unknown material's global sensitivity. The confirmation policy receives the scalar certificate, not the coefficients or clean response function.

Apparatus memory, confidence and preparation planning¶

With fixed final batch mass, actual composition is

[ z_t=(1-r_t)x_t+r_t h_{t-1},\qquad r_t=\rho\eta^{k_t},\qquad h_t=(1-\lambda)h_{t-1}+\lambda z_t. ]

Fresh preparation measures the nominal candidate independently and leaves the shared line's residual unchanged. Under candidate-only shared-line actions and externally valid bounds, define

[ \bar r_t=\bar\rho\bar\eta^{k_t},\quad D_t=[1-\underline\lambda(1-\bar r_t)]D_{t-1},\quad B_t=L\bar r_tD_{t-1},\quad D_0=2. ]

Then the latent observation differs from the fresh candidate response by at most(B_t). Fresh actions have (B_t=0) and do not change (D_t). For a schedule and selection of observations fixed before confirmation outcomes, independent Gaussian noise gives the fixed-final interval

[ \bar Y\ \pm\ \left[\bar B+1.959963984540054\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right]. ]

This interval has conditional coverage at least 95% for the frozen candidate when all stated bounds and the noise assumption hold. It is not an optional-stopping or false-discovery-rate guarantee. A separate finite-horizon sub-Gaussian construction uses (\sigma\sqrt{2\log(2T/\alpha)/n}); it is not substituted silently into the fixed-final experiment.

The preplanned policy enumerates counts of routine, one-wash, three-wash and fresh candidate assays. For two adjacent retained bounds (r_a\le r_b), exchanging their order changes the total bias bound by

[ S_{ab}-S_{ba}=LD\underline\lambda(r_a-r_b)\le0, ]

while the downstream residual bound is unchanged. Thus strongest washes first minimize summed bias for fixed counts. The optimizer is exact only within this finite menu of fixed schedules using all observations with equal weights. The discard-four control is outside that class and can be better. Fresh placement is fixed last; placement equivalence applies only to the final equal-weight radius objective.

At equal fresh/routine cost, an all-fresh schedule has zero modeled bias and the largest affordable sample count. Any claimed advantage of shared-line preparation must therefore be conditional on cost assumptions.

def block(distance, count, washes, info):
    """Summed predictable bias bound and final state-distance bound."""
    if count==0:
        return 0.0,distance
    retained=info.rho_upper*info.eta_upper**washes
    q=1-info.lambda_lower*(1-retained)
    power=q**count
    geometric=(1-power)/(1-q)
    return info.lipschitz_l1*retained*distance*geometric,distance*power

def optimize_plan(info):
    """Exhaustively minimize final half-width in the declared finite menu."""
    info.validate()
    best=None
    best_key=None
    feasible_count=0
    b=info.budget
    c1=1+info.wash_cost
    c3=1+3*info.wash_cost
    for nf in range(int(math.floor(b/info.fresh_cost+1e-9))+1):
        after_f=b-nf*info.fresh_cost
        for n3 in range(int(math.floor(after_f/c3+1e-9))+1):
            after_3=after_f-n3*c3
            for n1 in range(int(math.floor(after_3/c1+1e-9))+1):
                after_1=after_3-n1*c1
                for nr in range(int(math.floor(after_1+1e-9))+1):
                    result=evaluate_counts(nr,n1,n3,nf,info)
                    if result is None: continue
                    feasible_count+=1
                    key=(result["half_width"],result["cost"],nf,result["wash_operations"],-nr)
                    if best_key is None or key<best_key:
                        best_key=key
                        best=result
    if best is None:
        raise ValueError("No plan with at least two assays fits the budget")
    best["feasible_count_tuples"]=feasible_count
    best["order"]=[{"kind":"wash_candidate","washes":3,"fresh":False,"count":best["n_wash3"]},
                   {"kind":"wash_candidate","washes":1,"fresh":False,"count":best["n_wash1"]},
                   {"kind":"candidate","washes":0,"fresh":False,"count":best["n_routine"]},
                   {"kind":"fresh_candidate","washes":0,"fresh":True,"count":best["n_fresh"]}]
    best["inputs"]=asdict(info)
    return best

Execute every frozen computational experiment¶

The v1 and v2 scripts below are independent after preparation of the input data, so they run concurrently in two subprocesses. Both execute the full frozen seed lists and all methods. Their command lines, return codes, wall times and complete output logs are retained. No reduced-size demonstration run replaces the report experiments.

V1 uses report seeds 10000–10399, twelve regimes and ten policies. V2 uses report seeds 200000–200199 in each main case, and the declared first 100 seeds for each sensitivity. Development seeds remain separate. The v2 sensitivities include the Delaunay emulator, broad calibration bounds, empirical replicate-contrast noise and equal fresh/routine cost.

Reproducibility comparison against frozen originals¶

The following comparison reads the frozen originals only after the fresh computations finish. It checks complete raw result rows, numerical values and deterministic hashes. Time stamps and run-duration metadata are expected to differ and are not treated as scientific discrepancies.

In [10]:
comparisons=[]
for relative in ['research/trial_results.csv','research/v2/trial_results.csv',
                 'research/all_results_with_intervals.csv','research/v2/all_results_with_intervals.csv',
                 'research/paired_comparisons.csv','research/v2/paired_comparisons.csv']:
    original=pd.read_csv(PROJECT_ROOT/relative)
    rerun=pd.read_csv(RUN_ROOT/relative)
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(original,rerun,check_exact=True)
    comparison={'artifact':relative,'rows':len(rerun),'all_values_exactly_equal':True,
                'sha256_equal':sha256(PROJECT_ROOT/relative)==sha256(RUN_ROOT/relative),
                'rerun_sha256':sha256(RUN_ROOT/relative)}
    comparisons.append(comparison)
display(pd.DataFrame(comparisons))
assert all(r['sha256_equal'] for r in comparisons)
for relative in ['research/validation.json','research/v2/validation.json']:
    check=json.loads((RUN_ROOT/relative).read_text())
    assert check.get('all_checks_passed',check.get('all_data_checks_passed',False))
    display(Markdown(f'**{relative}: every integrity check passed.**'))

Full v1 results¶

Every method and regime is shown below. False confirmation uses all campaigns as its denominator; false fraction among accepts and sensitivity among truly qualifying candidates are separately available in the complete interval table. Zero observed events do not establish zero risk, and a degenerate paired bootstrap interval is not evidence of equivalence.

Executed benchmark results¶

The frozen study found sequence-dependent false confirmation, but did not establish an advantage for adaptive controls over a history model with simple candidate repetition.

The study used 400 independent seed draws (10000–10399), reused across 12 regimes, producing 48,000 policy runs for 10 methods. Regime-specific uncertainty respects this pairing. All candidate formulations were frozen after a shared 24-assay discovery campaign; every confirmation policy had the same 16-unit budget cap.

Three informative regimes¶

Rates below use all 400 campaigns as their denominator. Brackets give Wilson 95% intervals. Correct acceptance is a yield, not sensitivity conditional on a truly good recipe.

Primary comparison: active controls versus history-model repetition¶

This comparison uses the same inference model and discovery evidence. Both methods had zero false acceptances in every evaluated regime. For an individual 0/400 rate, the Wilson 95% upper bound is 0.95%; zero observed events do not establish zero risk. The paired bootstrap differences for this all-zero outcome are degenerate and must not be interpreted as an equivalence result.

Interpretation¶

  1. Replaying history can reproduce the wrong formulation. In nonlinear stress, predecessor-sequence replay produced 36 false confirmations out of 400 campaigns. Among its 267 accepted candidates, 36 were false (13.48%; Wilson 95% interval 9.90–18.10%). Ordinary candidate repetition produced 2/400 false confirmations, and history-model repetition produced 0/400. The requested recipe, preceding recipe and actual mixture are different objects.
  2. Candidate repetition is a strong control. Under last-mixture memory and a fixed repeated recipe, the composition discrepancy decays geometrically with each assay. A study that compares only with predecessor-sequence replay would overstate the need for adaptive action choice.
  3. Adaptive controls did not beat the strongest simple baseline. Under strong carryover, active controls accepted 229 truly good candidates, versus 235 for history-model repetition. The paired difference was −1.50 percentage points, with a 95% interval of −3.25 to +0.25. Under ineffective washing and costly washing the observed yield differences favored history-model repetition, but the multiple exploratory comparisons do not establish a universal ranking.
  4. Model misspecification remains consequential. Under nonlinear response stress, active controls and history-model repetition each correctly accepted 245/400 candidates. Active controls also falsely rejected 2 good candidates, versus none for history-model repetition. Its mean absolute fresh-response error was 0.01167, versus 0.00895; the paired increase was 0.00272, with a bootstrap 95% interval of 0.00174–0.00376. Fewer unresolved outcomes alone is not sufficient evidence of a better method.
  5. Costs change the amount of evidence purchased. Independent fresh assays cost four units by default, allowing four observations under the cap. Routine repetition permits sixteen. Fresh preparation removes modeled carryover but does not remove observation noise or the statistical difficulty of a near-threshold recipe. Costs are scenario assumptions, not measured laboratory time.
  6. The study supports a benchmark and a mechanism, with a negative result for the proposed action rule. The one-step covariance utility approximates clean-response variance reduction. It is not exact information gain, has no look-ahead, and does not explicitly minimize threshold decision error. These are plausible explanations to investigate in separately declared follow-up work, rather than conclusions identified causally by the present experiments.

Scope and uncertainty¶

All outcomes are from synthetic dimensionless response surfaces. The primary quadratic response family is included in the inference model; nonlinear response, long memory and off-grid carryover are explicit stress cases. Initial residual composition and observation noise are assumed known. Independent fresh preparation is an available measured action. The policy cannot see the true composition, carryover parameters or clean response used by the scorer.

The benchmark reports all campaigns, including weak discoveries; there was no post hoc restriction to apparently successful discovery runs. Illustrations use development seed 7, declared before evaluation, and are separate from evaluation estimates. Fixed wash/fresh-only policies can leave a remainder smaller than their scheduled next action; equal caps do not imply equal spend. First decision cost is a hypothetical threshold-crossing statistic from runs that continued to budget, not an early-stopping experiment.

See protocol.json for exact pre-evaluation commitments and pilot changes, trial_results.csv for every policy run, all_results_with_intervals.csv for the full rate/count/denominator table, paired_comparisons.csv for differences, and examples.json for complete fixed-development trajectories.

Full v2 main and sensitivity results¶

The table includes every policy in every case, with counts and intervals computed from the fresh rerun. Many discoveries already meet the illustrative target; true-good prevalence is therefore essential when interpreting a zero false-acceptance count. A zero denominator for invalid-candidate conditional rates is undefined, not zero.

V2 executed results¶

This extension combines measured OPV data, explicit response emulators and simulated carryover. The confidence construction certifies a fixed emulator under supplied bounds; it does not certify a physical OPV formulation from these data.

The frozen study completed3,200main campaign scenarios and1,600predeclared sensitivity scenarios, producing62,400policy runs. The same200 report seeds are reused across cases; uncertainty is calculated separately within case.

Held-out response fidelity¶

System Held-out groups MAE RMSE R² Emulator L1 certificate
pbq_qf 154 0.04390 0.05950 0.6062 1.66314
ptb7_th 154 0.05097 0.06732 0.4849 1.88188

These are modest prediction errors relative to the illustrative0.10 loss threshold. The fitted cubic family was prespecified and retained after held-out evaluation. These errors are not added to the emulator-only certificate, so the certificate cannot be transferred to real material response without additional validated model-error bounds.

Empirical coverage shortfall retained¶

The fixed-final mathematical construction did not yield nominal95% coverage in every finite simulation case. The following predeclared no-carryover case makes the observed shortfall explicit; common confirmation noise is reused across cases, so repeated low-carryover coverage values are not independent replications.

Method Covered / campaigns, with Wilson95% interval
bounded_repeat 188/200 (94.0%;95%CI89.8–96.5)
bounded_tail4 183/200 (91.5%;95%CI86.8–94.6)
bounded_fresh 186/200 (93.0%;95%CI88.6–95.8)
bounded_planner 188/200 (94.0%;95%CI89.8–96.5)

The retained audit_noise_coverage.py independently reconstructs the already-used stage21 Gaussian streams, with no new report seeds. The tail4 and fresh standardized errors reproduce their respective observed misses; the saved mean errors agree with the reconstructed noise to floating-point precision. No tail indexing or normalization defect was found. This check does not erase the empirical shortfall or establish empirical calibration; see coverage_noise_audit.json and coverage_noise_reconstruction.csv for exact counts, discrepancies and the finite-block diagnostic.

Interpretation boundaries¶

The planner is a preplanned preparation schedule, not an outcome-adaptive algorithm. Its exact optimality is restricted to enumerated routine/wash1/wash3/fresh count schedules using all their observations with equal weights. The prespecified discard-four control lies outside this class and can be better; this is why it remains a primary comparator.

Strong washes are placed first to reduce the accumulated worst-case bias bound. Fresh assays remove modeled carryover from their own observations while leaving the shared-line residual unchanged. With broad bounds, persistent memory or a large Delaunay Lipschitz certificate, the valid response interval can become conservative and fresh preparation may be selected. Such behavior reflects the supplied assumptions and costs, not measured OPV apparatus parameters.

At equal fresh/routine cost, an all-fresh schedule has zero modeled bias and the maximum affordable number of assays; it weakly dominates in the certified-width objective. The equal-cost sensitivity is included because no measured OPV cost data support the default four-unit fresh cost.

The empirical-contrast-noise sensitivity resamples symmetric half-differences of measured SDA pairs while still using assumed sigma0.03 in inference. It deliberately challenges the Gaussian/noise-bound assumption. Its coverage results are not covered by the main theorem, and this resampling is not a verified stochastic model of the laboratory.

Measured replicate disagreement, emulator prediction error and simulated carryover effects are separate evidence types. See the measured-data analysis for literal threshold reversals; neither those reversals nor interpolator roughness identifies carryover causally.

All methods and cases, exact counts/denominators, coverage and paired intervals are in summary.json, all_results_with_intervals.csv and paired_comparisons.csv. Every policy run is in trial_results.csv. Frozen configuration, scalar-only information boundary, source hashes and test/audit results are retained.

Limits and conclusions that the notebook can support¶

The v1 null comparison is retained: a complex adaptive control rule need not outperform repetition with the same history model. The v2 result is a conditional preparation-planning construction whose exact scope is a finite schedule menu and an equal-weight confidence radius. It is not a universal best policy. The physically meaningful questions are when the line can be cleared cheaply, how trustworthy the supplied calibration bounds are, and whether fresh preparation is actually more costly.

Measured response predictions have visible held-out errors. The theorem certifies the emulator, while the measured-data analysis reports literal replicate disagreements without causal attribution. Unknown true-material smoothness, unverified apparatus bounds, misspecified noise and unmeasured costs remain unresolved experimental requirements. None is hidden by a zero observed simulation error rate.

The complete proofs and qualifications are retained in the bundled theory note. All numerical statements in the result sections above are generated from the executed data.

What can be confirmed when preparation history is hidden?¶

Working theory note, 3 November 2026. These are elementary derivations and applications of established Lipschitz-extension and concentration arguments. They are not claimed as new mathematical theorems. The frozen baseline benchmark is unchanged; any implementation of these rules belongs to a separately specified extension.

1. Target, state and assumptions¶

Let x* be a nominal composition frozen after discovery and let theta = f(x*) be its mean response under an independent fresh preparation. Composition lies in a simplex. A norm must be fixed throughout; the simplex has diameter 2 in L1 and square root of 2 in L2.

For a shared-line preparation of x*, write

z_t = (1-r_t) x* + r_t h_(t-1)

and

h_t = (1-lambda_t) h_(t-1) + lambda_t z_t.

Here z_t is the actual mixture, h is residual composition and r_t is the retained fraction of the fixed final batch. Assume 0 <= r_t <= rbar_t < 1 and 0 < lambda_min <= lambda_t <= 1. Washes can justify rbar_t = rho_bar * eta_bar**k_t only when a valid bound eta_bar on the retained fraction after each wash is available. Without that information, a wash cannot be credited with a guaranteed reduction beyond the existing rho_bar bound.

Assume f is L-Lipschitz on the accessible composition domain in the chosen norm:

|f(u)-f(v)| <= L ||u-v||.

The assay is Y_t = f(z_t) + epsilon_t: preparation history is assumed to affect the mean only through actual composition. Additional drift, morphology changes or reaction pathways require their own valid bias bounds; otherwise this model does not cover them. For the concentration results, noise must satisfy the conditional moment-generating-function bound

E[exp(s epsilon_t) | F_(t-1), action_t] <= exp(s^2 sigma^2/2)

for every real s. Thus it is conditionally mean zero and sigma-sub-Gaussian. The action and its bias bound must be chosen from information available before observing epsilon_t. Independent Gaussian noise with known standard deviation sigma is a sufficient special case. An independent fresh preparation has z_t = x*, bias zero and leaves the shared-line state unchanged.

These assumptions are inputs requiring physical calibration or a justified model. They are not consequences of a successful simulation or a well-fitting regression. If an emulator is clipped to a physical range, clip its latent response before adding zero-mean noise; clipping the noisy observation itself generally introduces bias.

2. Natural flushing and a deterministic bias envelope¶

Subtracting x* from the state update gives the exact identity

h_t-x* = [1-lambda_t(1-r_t)] (h_(t-1)-x*).

For constant rho and lambda with no washing, q = 1-lambda(1-rho). Therefore h_t-x* = q**t (h_0-x*). The matched lambda = 1 model contracts by rho. At rho = 0.40 and lambda = 0.45 the contraction factor is 0.73. Here h_0 denotes the state at the beginning of the confirmation repetition sequence, not necessarily the known initial priming state before discovery.

If D_(t-1) >= ||h_(t-1)-x*||, a valid observable envelope is

B_t = L rbar_t D_(t-1)

D_t = [1-lambda_min(1-rbar_t)] D_(t-1).

Then |f(z_t)-theta| <= B_t and ||h_t-x*|| <= D_t. The proof is the identity above, monotonicity in retained fraction and the Lipschitz inequality. A conservative initial D_0 is the simplex diameter; a tighter calibrated initial-state bound may be used. For a fresh action use B_t = 0 and D_t = D_(t-1).

For constant bounds rho_bar and lambda_min, let qbar = 1-lambda_min(1-rho_bar). After b discarded routine repeats and m further unwashed repeats, the mean systematic error is bounded by

Bbar_(b,m) = L rho_bar D_0 qbar**b (1-qbar**m) / [m(1-qbar)].

This follows by summing a geometric series. If qbar = 1, use the limit instead; the bound does not decay with repetitions. The result requires a positive lower bound on lambda and an upper bound below one on retained fraction for geometric contraction. A favorable posterior mean of these parameters does not supply such bounds.

A final mixture can be nearly fresh while the average of every earlier assay remains biased. Prespecified burn-in and tail averaging are consequently essential simple controls, alongside same-model repetition.

3. Fixed-horizon and adaptive confidence intervals¶

Write b_t = f(z_t)-theta, so |b_t| <= B_t. For n target assays let Ybar_n = sum(Y_t)/n and Bbar_n = sum(B_t)/n.

Fixed sample size¶

If n is fixed before observing the confirmation outcomes, the sub-Gaussian tail bound gives

theta in [Ybar_n - Bbar_n - R_n, Ybar_n + Bbar_n + R_n]

with probability at least 1-alpha, where

R_n = sigma sqrt[2 log(2/alpha)/n].

The same statement holds for a fixed tail window after prespecified burn-in. Under independent Gaussian noise, z_(1-alpha/2) sigma / sqrt(n) replaces R_n for a tighter fixed-sample interval. Neither expression may be reused for unrestricted repeated peeking without a correction.

Adaptive actions and stopping up to T target assays¶

For a predeclared maximum T, use

R_n = sigma sqrt[2 log(2T/alpha)/n], for n = 1,...,T.

The intervals using this R_n and Bbar_n cover theta simultaneously with probability at least 1-alpha. Thus wash/fresh choices can depend on previous measurements and the study may stop at any n <= T.

Proof: iterated conditional moment-generating-function bounds imply P(|sum_(t=1)^n epsilon_t| >= sigma sqrt[2n log(2T/alpha)]) <= alpha/T for each fixed n. A union bound over n yields simultaneous control. On that event, the triangle inequality and |sum b_t| <= sum B_t give every stated interval. The bias bounds may be random and depend on previous outcomes because their inequality holds pathwise; noise must retain the stated conditional bound.

For the claim theta >= tau, accept only when the lower endpoint is at least tau, reject only when the upper endpoint is below tau and otherwise remain unresolved. Under the assumptions, any wrong threshold conclusion over the entire horizon occurs with probability at most alpha. This is conditional on one frozen candidate and valid assumptions; it is not a guarantee against arbitrary unmodeled laboratory behavior. Repeatedly replacing the candidate until one is accepted requires a separate multiple-candidate error budget.

This controls error probability over repetitions of the specified confirmation procedure. It does not imply that at most alpha of the accepted claims will be false: the false fraction among accepted claims also depends on candidate prevalence and acceptance power. Report those quantities separately.

Selecting a tail window after seeing data¶

A post hoc choice of burn-in or a favorable tail must also be accounted for. There are M = T(T+1)/2 contiguous windows. For every window s,...,t of length m, use

R_(s,t) = sigma sqrt[2 log(2M/alpha)/m]

and its own mean response and mean bias bound. A union bound makes all these intervals valid simultaneously. Any one window can then be selected adaptively or their intersection can be used. If the intersection is empty, report incompatible evidence and do not manufacture a point estimate or confidence claim. This simple construction is conservative; sharper time-uniform methods are established in the confidence-sequence literature [Howard et al., 2021; existing source 10].

If calibrated physical bounds hold only with probability at least 1-delta, a separate union bound yields coverage at least 1-alpha-delta. This requires a justified joint calibration statement; it cannot turn an empirical slope estimate into a global smoothness guarantee.

4. Exact finite-data Lipschitz envelopes¶

Suppose actual query points z_i and noiseless responses y_i are known. Assume their pairwise values are L-consistent: |y_i-y_j| <= L ||z_i-z_j||. Every L-Lipschitz function agreeing with the data obeys

lower(x*) = max_i [y_i - L ||z_i-x*||]

upper(x*) = min_i [y_i + L ||z_i-x*||].

These bounds are sharp over the class. To see this, define on the whole domain

f_lower(x) = max_i [y_i - L ||z_i-x||]

and

f_upper(x) = min_i [y_i + L ||z_i-x||].

Each function is L-Lipschitz. Pairwise consistency makes both interpolate every y_i. They attain the respective endpoints at x*. Convex combinations of these two functions realize every intermediate value while retaining the same data and Lipschitz constant. This is an application of the classical real-valued Lipschitz extension construction associated with McShane, not a new extension theorem.

Consequently, the data force theta >= tau only if lower(x*) >= tau and force theta < tau only if upper(x*) < tau. Otherwise both conclusions are compatible with the stated function class. A model-based point prediction inside the interval does not remove this ambiguity.

For simultaneous measurement bands ell_i <= f(z_i) <= u_i, replace y_i by ell_i in the lower envelope and by u_i in the upper envelope. When the bands admit an L-Lipschitz function, the same construction shows sharpness. These envelopes concern uncertainty in function values at known actual locations. If actual locations are hidden but ||z_i-x*|| <= D_i is guaranteed, replacing each distance by D_i yields valid conservative bounds; sharpness generally disappears because it ignores joint constraints on possible hidden trajectories.

5. What finite smooth data alone cannot identify¶

Smoothness without a known quantitative bound does not determine the fresh response from a finite transcript. Grant the observer even the actual query set Z = {z_1,...,z_n} and suppose x* is absent from Z. Let d be the minimum distance from x* to Z and choose radius r < d. There is a smooth bump b supported in the ball of radius r around x*, with b(x*) = 1 and b(z_i) = 0. For example, inside the ball use

b(x) = e * exp[-1/(1-||x-x*||_2^2/r^2)],

and use zero outside. Restricting this smooth ambient function to a boundary of the simplex is permitted.

For any smooth compatible f_0, the functions f_0 + Delta*b agree at every observed actual point and can differ arbitrarily at x*. Two offsets can place their target values on opposite sides of tau. For a fixed noiseless adaptive transcript, the same observed path is obtained by induction because each previously queried response is unchanged. With noise, the construction establishes equal likelihood conditional on those locations or pathwise compatibility under the same realized noise.

This is finite-transcript underdetermination, not a claim that every randomized-design statistical model is globally unidentifiable. A restrictive finite-dimensional response family, a quantitative Lipschitz bound or a direct fresh measurement supplies additional information. The frozen quadratic benchmark has precisely such strong structural assumptions.

6. A reviewable extension policy¶

Keep the frozen baseline intact. A conservative extension can compare a finite menu of plans: independent fresh repeats; fixed burn-in followed by ordinary candidate repeats; and fixed burn-in followed by k washes before each candidate assay. Choose the plan minimizing the proved interval half-width subject to the declared cost cap. For wash plan k, use rbar = rho_bar eta_bar**k and qbar_k = 1-lambda_min(1-rbar) in the geometric sum. Charge discarded burn-in assays, wash operations and every fresh assay.

For adaptive operation, maintain D_t and all B_t values, choose actions using any prespecified rule and base conclusions on the simultaneous interval. An approximate action planner does not invalidate coverage if its choices are predictable and the physical/noise assumptions hold. Its efficiency still needs comparison against fresh-only, fixed washed repeats, same-model repetition and prespecified tail averages. An action rule based on interval width or look-ahead is a research proposal, not a demonstrated new algorithm or a guaranteed improvement.

7. What measured materials data can establish¶

The maximum observed pairwise slope in a dataset is a lower bound on any Lipschitz constant consistent with those data. It is not an upper bound on an unknown material response between samples. Independent physical knowledge, additional regularity assumptions or a certified bound for a specifically defined emulator is needed. A bound proved for an emulator certifies that emulator, not its approximation to a real material.

Using measured organic-photovoltaic formulation outcomes to construct a response surface can add a concrete application. If carryover, wash efficacy and assay noise are subsequently simulated, describe the study as a measured-data-anchored emulator with synthetic preparation history. Claims about actual carryover in that materials system require corresponding measurements. The physical assumptions, emulator error and confirmation error are three distinct sources of uncertainty.

8. A computable Lipschitz certificate for a Bernstein emulator¶

Let a K-component composition lie in the unit simplex and define a degree-p standard multivariate Bernstein polynomial

f(x) = sum_(|alpha|=p) beta_alpha B_alpha^p(x),

where B_alpha^p(x) = (p! / product_i alpha_i!) product_i x_i**alpha_i. All multi-indices of total degree p must be included. Its ambient polynomial derivative is

partial_i f(x) = p sum_(|gamma|=p-1) beta_(gamma+e_i) B_gamma^(p-1)(x).

For any vector c and tangent direction v with sum_i v_i = 0,

|c dot v| <= (max_i c_i - min_i c_i) ||v||_1 / 2.

Proof: subtract the midpoint of the largest and smallest c_i from every component; the subtraction does not change c dot v and Hölder's inequality bounds the result. The factor one half is attained by transferring equal opposite mass between a maximal and minimal coordinate.

For each gradient difference, Bernstein weights are nonnegative and sum to one on the simplex. Therefore a valid global L1 Lipschitz constant is

L_certificate = (p/2) max_(|gamma|=p-1, i,j) |beta_(gamma+e_i)-beta_(gamma+e_j)|.

Integrating the bounded directional derivative along the straight segment between any two simplex points proves the Lipschitz inequality. This is an upper bound; it need not be the smallest possible constant. It is computable from fitted coefficients and does not depend on unobserved material labels.

Use normalized composition fractions summing to one. Transforming the response by an affine scaling multiplies the certificate by the absolute scale factor. Clipping the polynomial response to a fixed interval cannot increase its Lipschitz constant. Recompute the certificate from the final fitted coefficients after any train-plus-validation refit. The certificate concerns this mathematical emulator on the chosen simplex; held-out prediction error and correspondence to real materials must be evaluated separately. A conservative certificate may produce wide intervals and few decisions; that outcome must remain visible.

9. Optimal ordering for a specified fixed-schedule bound¶

Consider only candidate assays, with known costs, the same noise bound sigma and a common memory lower bound lambda_min. Every observation is retained with equal weight. An action has retained-fraction upper bound r and state-contraction bound q(r) = 1-lambda_min(1-r). No additional order-dependent costs or feasibility restrictions are assumed.

Given state-distance bound D before two adjacent shared-line actions a and b, their total bias-bound contribution is

S_ab = L D [r_a + r_b q(r_a)].

Reversing their order gives

S_ab - S_ba = L D lambda_min (r_a-r_b).

Their final state bound is D q(r_a) q(r_b), which is the same in either order. Every later contribution is therefore unchanged. If r_a <= r_b, placing a before b cannot increase the total bound. Repeatedly swapping inverted adjacent pairs proves that, for fixed action counts, ascending retained fraction—strongest washing first—minimizes the summed bias bound. This is a direct exchange argument for this model and objective; no first-ever scheduling theorem is claimed.

A block of n identical shared actions contributes

L r D (1-q(r)**n)/(1-q(r))

and leaves state bound D q(r)**n. Use the limiting value L r D n when q(r) = 1. Fresh actions add zero bias and do not change D. Their position is irrelevant to this final-width objective, although it can affect early stopping behavior and must be fixed if such outcomes are reported.

For a finite action menu, enumerate all nonnegative count vectors satisfying the cost cap and a prespecified minimum number of assays. For each vector, sort the shared actions as proved above, compute total bias bound S and let N count all shared and fresh observations. Under independent Gaussian noise and a plan chosen before confirmation outcomes, minimize

H = S/N + z_(1-alpha/2) sigma/sqrt(N).

The result minimizes the certified fixed-final confidence half-width within this explicitly defined class. Finite enumeration is possible because every action has positive cost. A different noise radius depending only on N can be substituted without changing the ordering argument.

This is not a global optimum among tail-discarding, weighted, model-based or outcome-adaptive policies. Discarding burn-in changes which contributions appear in S and a prespecified burn-in/tail-average baseline remains essential. Nor does minimum worst-case width guarantee best realized prediction error or lowest decision cost. Those are empirical comparisons. The old frozen benchmark is preserved; this schedule analysis belongs to the separately specified extension.

10. When inexpensive repetition can beat independent preparation¶

This is a sufficient comparison within the assumed scalar model. It is not a general claim that repeating a contaminated preparation is preferable in a laboratory.

Assume valid constant bounds with 0 <= qbar < 1, fixed L, rho_bar and D0, independent Gaussian errors with known sigma > 0, plus 0 < alpha < 1. Define z = z_(1-alpha/2) and

C = L rho_bar D0/(1-qbar).

With n routine candidate assays and every observation retained, the exact mean-bias bound is C(1-qbar**n)/n <= C/n. Consequently

H_repeat <= C/n + z sigma/sqrt(n).

The transient bias contribution is O(1/n) for fixed valid bounds, whereas the Gaussian averaging term is O(n**(-1/2)). This asymptotic comparison is about increasing affordable assay counts. It does not ensure a useful bias bound at a fixed small budget. A qbar close to one can make C large.

Let routine cost be one. If the same budget permits n routine assays or exactly n/c fresh assays, where c > 1 and n/c is an admissible integer count, then

H_fresh = z sigma sqrt(c)/sqrt(n).

A conservative sufficient condition for the repeat-radius upper bound to be strictly smaller is

sqrt(n) > C/[z sigma (sqrt(c)-1)].

Derivation: subtract the repeat Gaussian term from the fresh radius and compare the remaining quantity with C/n. Multiplication by n gives C < z sigma (sqrt(c)-1) sqrt(n). This condition compares certified radii, not realized mean absolute error or acceptance yield.

For arbitrary positive action costs and integer budget remainders, use the actual feasible counts n and m. Provided 1 <= m < n, the corresponding sufficient condition is

C/n < z sigma [1/sqrt(m)-1/sqrt(n)].

The planner uses its exact feasible-count objective rather than either sufficient approximation. If fresh and routine costs are equal, fresh observations attain the same sample count with zero preparation bias and therefore weakly dominate this menu in certified fixed-final width. If sigma is zero, these divisions by sigma do not apply; fresh preparation has zero radius under the idealized model and routine preparation can at most tie it when its bias bound is zero.

11. A conditional power bound for a fixed plan¶

Fix the confirmation sample count n and a deterministic valid mean-bias bound Bbar. Assume independent Gaussian errors with known sigma > 0. If theta = tau + Delta with Delta > 0, acceptance requires

Ybar - Bbar - z sigma/sqrt(n) >= tau.

Write Ybar = theta + bbar + epsilonbar, where |bbar| <= Bbar. The event

epsilonbar >= 2 Bbar + z sigma/sqrt(n) - Delta

is sufficient for acceptance for every admissible bias. Since epsilonbar/(sigma/sqrt(n)) is standard Gaussian,

P(accept) >= Phi[(Delta-2 Bbar) sqrt(n)/sigma-z].

For a failing target theta = tau-Delta, the analogous lower bound holds for rejection by using the least favorable bias +Bbar. The statement holds conditional on the frozen discovery record with the same valid physical bounds. It is a lower bound, not an estimate of actual power or a power calculation for the proposed physical pilot. Smaller Bbar helps the guarantee, but a more expensive preparation can reduce n enough to offset that improvement. For random data-selected n or bias bounds, this particular fixed-plan expression cannot be reused without a justified conditioning or sequential argument.
